newsitem.title: FRANCE: Albright seeks NATO reaffirmation on expansion.
newsitem.headline: Albright seeks NATO reaffirmation on expansion.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright attends her first NATO foreign ministers' meeting on Tuesday seeking reaffirmation the alliance is united on eastward expansion before she talks to Russian leaders later this week.

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said that as the Russians were talking tough in negotiations on a new post-Cold War relationship with NATO and "because they are trying out different things on different people, she feels a need to make sure that NATO remains unified".
A NATO foreign ministers' meeting was "one way to do that. It's not portent of any kind of crisis. It's just good politics," Burns told reporters.

Albright was due to travel to Brussels early on Tuesday after talks in Paris on Monday that warmed the tone and style, if not the substance, of often prickly Franco-American relations. She was to meet European Union officials first, then head to NATO.
The first woman appointed America's top diplomat, Albright was kissed by French leaders in Paris and warmly cooed over by German and Italian leaders on earlier stops in Bonn and Rome.
Possibly the first U.S. secretary of state with fluency in several languages, she spoke French publicly and with French leaders and even answered a reporter's question in Russian.

Three days into her first overseas trip -- an 11-day whirlwind tour of nine major capitals in Europe and Asia -- European media have hailed the 59-year-old grandmother as an "Iron Lady" who is an energetic contrast to her more cautious predecessor, Warren Christopher.
There have also been media complants that her belief in the United States as the "indispensable nation" in world affairs undergirds a kind of American "velvet hegemony".
During her stops in France, Germany and Italy, Albright did not duck differences with allies on issues such as NATO internal reform plans, trade with Iran and Scientology.

But her main message, and that of her hosts, was that the alliance was firmly set for a planned July summit in Madrid when NATO leaders would decide which former Warsaw Pact states would join the alliance as the first post-Cold War members.
It is generally accepted that Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic will be asked to join. The question is whether others will be added to that list.

France is pushing to include Romania but U.S. officials say this is "a long shot". Paris also wants Slovenia included, and the U.S. Pentagon sees a military logic to that choice. But one U.S. official put Slovenia's admission chances at 60 percent.

NATO Secretary General Javier Solana is leading negotiations with Moscow on a charter defining Russia's special relationship with the alliance into the millennium. That document will be a major focus of Tuesday's NATO meeting.

Many NATO foreign ministers have met Russian leaders recently or, like Albright, will do so in the near future as part of a campaign to persuade Moscow that an expanded alliance will help stabilise Europe, not threaten Russia.

To that end, Albright was expected to brief the Russians on a new U.S. study which anticipated extra U.S. defence spending due to NATO expansion would cost no more than $200 million annually and assumed that no alliance forces would be permanently deployed in the new NATO states, U.S. officials said.
She was also expected to brief the Russians on a new NATO conventional arms reduction proposal, if it was approved before her visit.
